summary:
Round 2, scoped to the one new test added since round 1: anUncontendedReleaseDoesNotWedgeTheLockForALaterThread in sequencer/src/test/java/binjava/sequencer/LeaseManagerConcurrencyTest.java. Traced the claimed mutation by hand against the current LeaseManager.java and BoundedLock.java: negating `if (!lock.tryLock())` to `if (lock.tryLock())` in release() (LeaseManager.java:419-421) makes the uncontended path call tryLock() (succeeds, hold count 1) and then also takeOrFail (reentrant, succeeds instantly, hold count 2); the unchanged `finally { lock.unlock(); }` only drops it to 1, so the releasing thread returns holding the lock forever. The test's releaser thread (uncontended, on a fresh LeaseManager/MemoryBinStore, no gate needed) then joins cleanly under the mutant (release() does not throw), but the second, different-thread prober's tryAcquire() then blocks on BoundedLock.takeOrFail('acquire', renewInterval) against a lock owned by a thread that already returned and will never unlock again, times out after renewInterval, and throws IOException -- failing 'the probing thread did not throw' (and, had it not, 'acquired' would be empty). Confirmed this is the only test in the diff that can see this: every other release-touching test (single-threaded release-then-something-else, or the existing in-flight-acquire interleave test) either reuses the SAME thread afterward -- for which ReentrantLock reentrancy masks a stray extra hold -- or is itself killed earlier by the same mutation for an unrelated reason (in the contended interleave test, the negated condition skips takeOrFail entirely on the contended path and the subsequent unowned unlock() throws IllegalMonitorStateException, caught by that test's own releaseFailed assertion). So the new test closes a real, distinct gap rather than duplicating existing coverage.

Checked for a weaker-mutation blind spot as directed: a hypothetical implementation that double-locks AND double-unlocks (fully benign, net hold count still 0) is correctly NOT flagged by this test, because the test asserts observable behaviour (a second thread can still take the lock) rather than counting lock/unlock call sites -- this is the correct shape of test, not a gap. Also checked whether BoundedLock.tryLock() being stubbed to always return false (bypassing the fast path, always falling through to takeOrFail) survives this test: it does, since takeOrFail on an uncontended real lock still succeeds near-instantly and the net effect is unchanged -- but that mutation only removes a performance optimisation, not a correctness property, and no assertion in this task claims to cover it, so it is not a finding.

Sanity-checked the two 10-second joins against the class's @Timeout(60, SEPARATE_THREAD): JUnit 5 applies a class-level @Timeout as the per-METHOD default, not a budget shared across the class's methods, so the real worst case for this test alone is two sequential timeouts (~20s under the mutant, sub-second under correct code) against its own independent 60s budget -- comfortable margin either way, and no flakiness risk from CI load given both operations are in-memory. (Note: the framing that the 60s bound must contain 'two sequential 10-second joins plus the rest of the test suite in that class' rests on treating the timeout as class-summed, which is not how @Timeout works; noted for accuracy, not raised as a finding since the test is not flaky under either reading.)

Confirmed BoundedLockTest.java is not present in the staged index (`git ls-files -s` on the review's GIT_INDEX_FILE) and not present as a .java source anywhere in the working tree. The only trace is gitignored build cruft (an empty sequencer/build/reports/tests/test/binjava.sequencer.BoundedLockTest report directory and a stray compiled .class in compileTestJava's stash-dir), both matched by .gitignore's build/ rule and irrelevant to the commit. Not a finding.

No assertion in the new test was weakened relative to anything -- it is new. No blocking or major findings.
